analysis.one_liner: Lets workers unionize by signing cards instead of an election, and adds penalties for employers who interfere.
analysis.headline: Backed by 46 senators and the Democratic presidential field, the bill was referred to committee and never received a vote in the Senate.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed three things about how unions form. If a majority of workers at a workplace signed cards saying they wanted a union, the government would certify it directly instead of holding an election. If a company and a newly certified union could not agree on a first contract, a mediator and then an arbitrator would impose one. And employers who fired or threatened workers for supporting a union would face much stiffer penalties, including fines up to $20,000 per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers trying to form or join a union. If a majority of employees in a workplace signed cards designating a union, the National Labor Relations Board would certify the union directly instead of requiring an employer-requested election [S2][S3]. If bargaining for a first contract stalled, the dispute would go to mediation and then to binding arbitration, so an employer could not simply refuse to agree to any contract [S3]. Workers fired or threatened for supporting a union during an organizing drive would get priority investigations, double back pay plus liquidated damages, and employers would face civil penalties of up to $20,000 per violation [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Workers could certify a union once a majority signed authorization cards, skipping the election period during which employers commonly campaign against the union.
Workers at a newly certified union could not be left without a contract: after 90 days of bargaining and 30 days of mediation, a binding arbitration panel would set the first contract for two years.

Workers fired or threatened for union activity during an organizing drive would get priority investigation of their complaints, double back pay plus liquidated damages, and employers would face civil penalties up to $20,000 per violation.

analysis.who_pays: Employers. They would face union certification without an election if a majority of workers signed cards, binding arbitration to settle a first contract, doubled back-pay awards plus liquidated damages for firing or threatening union supporters, and civil penalties of up to $20,000 per violation during organizing drives [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Card-check certification replaces a private-ballot election with signed public cards, which critics across the political spectrum argue exposes workers to pressure from whichever side approaches them first — union organizers or co-workers — rather than a private vote.

Binding arbitration of first contracts lets a government-appointed panel set wages and work rules for two years even when the parties cannot agree, removing negotiated consent from the initial employment terms.
The new $20,000 penalties apply only to employers, not to unions, for misconduct during organizing drives.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers seeking a union, the bill addressed the best-documented weaknesses of the current system: the months between filing and election in which employers can legally campaign against a union, and the fact that a large share of first contracts are never signed because an employer can simply refuse to bargain. The main cost falls on employers, who would lose the election stage and face real financial consequences for illegal retaliation. The strongest objection is design, not cost: replacing elections with signed cards trades one pressure problem (employer intimidation, which the bill penalizes) for another (signing under public scrutiny), and imposed first contracts substitute an arbitrator's judgment for bargaining. Those are serious, debatable trade-offs, but the bill died before any of them were tested in a vote or amended.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and sat there without ever being brought to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Kennedy introduced the bill on March 29, 2007, with 46 original cosponsors, all Democrats or left-leaning independents.
The bill was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never received a vote or any further Senate action.
The bill would have let the National Labor Relations Board certify a union without an election if a majority of workers signed authorization cards.
The bill would have sent stalled first-contract negotiations to mediation and then to binding arbitration lasting two years.
The bill would have added doubled back pay, liquidated damages, and civil penalties of up to $20,000 per violation for employers who fire or threaten workers during union drives.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and business groups that opposed the bill. The existing system remained in place: unions generally still had to win an election, and penalties for firing or threatening union supporters stayed modest.

for.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 46 original cosponsors

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and allied business groups
against.what_they_did: Led business opposition to card-check certification and mandatory first-contract arbitration, arguing elections by secret ballot should remain and arbitrators should not set contract terms

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill and prevented it from reaching the floor; the Senate took no recorded action on it beyond referral in the provided record

sides.party_line_note: All 47 initial sponsors were Democrats or left-leaning independents (46 cosponsors: 44 Democrats, 1 Independent, 1 Independent Democrat); opposition, though not recorded in a roll call in the action history, came from Republicans and business groups.

industries.industry: Employers across union-organizable sectors (manufacturing, retail, hospitality, logistics)
industries.note: The bill's core provisions fall directly on employers: card-check certification, binding arbitration of first contracts, and fines up to $20,000 per violation during organizing drives. Employers' interest in defeating the bill ran against the workers it was meant to protect.
Card-check certification and binding first-contract arbitration would have made organizing dramatically easier and faster, directly increasing unions' membership and revenue base.

industries.industry: Union-avoidance consultants and labor-relations law firms
industries.note: A large consulting industry helps employers defeat union campaigns; card-check certification and stiffer penalties for interference would have reduced the value of that work. (General knowledge, not in the provided sources.)
